Cycle, ovulation,
and fertility in PCOS
8 min read
Guide
Intermediate
Reviewed content

With PCOS, your cycle can become long, irregular, and sometimes hard to predict. Understanding what happens around ovulation can help you make sense of your cycle and better understand fertility-related questions.
In this article
Why the cycle becomes irregular
What happens around ovulation
How to recognize ovulation
PCOS and fertility
Why apps may be less accurate
Tracking your cycle with PCOS
When to see a doctor if you want to conceive
Key takeaways
The menstrual cycle depends on a coordinated sequence of hormonal signals. In PCOS, this organization can be disrupted, particularly in follicle development and ovulation.

The ovaries can contain many small follicles that begin developing without a dominant follicle regularly reaching maturity. Ovulation may then be delayed, occur unpredictably, or not happen at all during certain cycles.
This is one of the reasons some people with PCOS have cycles of 35, 45, or sometimes more days, while others may have cycles closer to a typical length.
Good to know
Cycle length alone doesn’t tell you whether ovulation occurred. Two cycles of the same length can have a different hormonal story.
Ovulation is the release of an egg from an ovary. It follows a phase of follicular maturation and precedes the luteal phase of the cycle.
In a regular cycle, ovulation is often around the midpoint. But with PCOS, this simple rule doesn’t always apply. Ovulation may be much later or may not happen at all in a given cycle.
Why this matters
When ovulation is unpredictable, it becomes harder to estimate the fertile window based on period dates alone.
There are several physical signs that can accompany the hormonal changes around ovulation. They can be useful for observing your own cycle, but no single sign can confirm ovulation with certainty.
A change in cervical mucus, which may become more abundant, clear, and stretchy
Mild pelvic pain or discomfort in some women
A change in body temperature after ovulation
A change in vaginal wetness
A possible increase in libido in some women

Cervical mucus is particularly worth observing. As the fertile window approaches, it may become more abundant, clear, slippery, and stretchy. However, its appearance can vary from person to person and from cycle to cycle.
Be careful with predictions
With very irregular cycles, an ovulation date calculated automatically from previous cycles can be very approximate. A prediction is not a medical confirmation of ovulation.
PCOS can make conception more difficult, mainly when ovulation is infrequent or hard to predict. However, having PCOS doesn’t mean being infertile.
Some women with PCOS ovulate regularly and conceive without particular difficulty. For others, ovulation is irregular enough to call for an evaluation and possibly medical care.
PCOS doesn’t automatically cause infertility
The main difficulty is often irregular or unpredictable ovulation
Ovulation can occur even when cycles are very long
Appropriate care can improve the chances of conception
The fertility journey depends on each individual and many other factors

Fertility doesn’t depend on ovulation alone, either. Age, partner sperm quality, the condition of the fallopian tubes, the endometrium, and other factors can also play a role. This is why a comprehensive evaluation matters when pregnancy takes longer than expected.
Period-tracking apps generally use data from previous cycles to produce estimates. When cycles are relatively regular, these estimates can be useful as a reference.
With PCOS, however, cycle variability can make these calculations less reliable. An app cannot know for certain that ovulation has occurred just because a theoretical date has been reached.
Use it as a reference point
Digital tracking is most useful for observing trends in your own cycle and keeping a history to share with your healthcare provider.
Regular tracking can help you better understand your personal variations. The goal isn’t to make the cycle perfectly predictable, but rather to gather enough information to identify trends.
Note the date of the first day of each cycle, even when cycles are very spaced out
Observe changes in cervical mucus throughout the cycle
Note any pelvic pain or other signs that may accompany ovulation
Avoid relying solely on an average 28-day length to predict ovulation
Use ovulation tests with caution and, if needed, ask a professional for advice
Share the information you gather with a healthcare professional if you want to become pregnant

It can also help to note associated symptoms: pain, acne, changes in mucus, unusual bleeding, mood, sleep, or other personal observations. This information can help build a fuller picture of your cycle.
A consultation can be worthwhile even before starting to try to conceive, when cycles are very irregular, very spaced out, or when periods are absent for an extended time.
A healthcare professional can investigate the causes of the irregularities, assess ovulation, and if needed, suggest a strategy suited to your pregnancy plans.
When to seek advice
If your periods are very spaced out, if you haven’t had a period for several months, or if pregnancy doesn’t happen despite regular intercourse, talk to a healthcare professional.
Key points
PCOS can make cycles long and unpredictable.
Ovulation may be irregular or absent in some cycles.
An irregular cycle doesn’t automatically mean a lack of fertility.
Predictions based solely on the calendar may be less reliable with PCOS.
Observing your cycle and keeping a history can be useful, especially for a consultation.
One last word
PCOS doesn’t show up the same way in every woman. Your cycle may change over time. Tracking is there to help you better understand how your body works, not to replace medical advice.
This article is for informational and educational purposes only. It does not constitute a medical diagnosis and does not replace a consultation with a healthcare professional.

PCOS diagnosis:
tests and workup
7 min read
Guide
Intermediate
Reviewed content
How PCOS is diagnosed, what tests may be offered, and how to prepare calmly for your appointment.
In this article
Understanding the diagnostic workup
The main steps of the workup
The hormonal blood test
The pelvic ultrasound
What the diagnosis doesn’t tell you
Preparing for your appointment
Key takeaways

The diagnosis of polycystic ovary syndrome doesn’t rely on a single test. The healthcare professional brings together several pieces of information: your cycle history, any symptoms, the clinical exam, lab tests, and, depending on the situation, an ultrasound.
The goal is both to look for features consistent with PCOS and to rule out other causes that could explain irregular periods or certain hormonal symptoms.
Good to know
The diagnosis is always personalized. Two women with PCOS can have very different symptoms and test results.
The workup can follow several steps. They aren’t necessarily all carried out the same way for everyone.
History-taking
The professional gathers your history: cycles, symptoms, medical background, and treatments.
Clinical exam
They look in particular for signs of excess androgens and assess your overall condition.
Blood workup
Hormonal and metabolic tests may be requested to clarify the situation.
Ultrasound
It can complete the workup by observing the appearance of the ovaries.
The process at a glance
History and symptoms
Clinical exam
Tests depending on the situation
Ultrasound if needed
A blood test may be offered to look for signs of excess androgens, assess certain hormones involved in reproductive function, and look for other possible causes of your symptoms.
The tests chosen depend on your age, your symptoms, your medical history, and what the professional is looking to check.
Androgens
Testosterone and other hormones depending on the situation.
Thyroid function
Helps in particular rule out certain causes of irregular cycles.
Metabolic workup
Blood glucose, sometimes a lipid panel depending on risk factors.
Important
Hormonal results need to be interpreted alongside the clinical context. A single value usually isn’t enough, on its own, to conclude a PCOS diagnosis.

An ultrasound can be used to observe the appearance of the ovaries and look in particular for a high number of small follicles. It also allows the professional to look for other factors that could explain certain symptoms.
Good to know
Seeing many follicles on ultrasound doesn’t automatically mean you have PCOS. The result needs to be interpreted alongside the rest of the workup.
Receiving a PCOS diagnosis doesn’t make it possible to predict exactly how things will progress for you. The syndrome can show up very differently from one person to another.
PCOS doesn’t automatically mean infertility.
PCOS doesn’t necessarily mean having cysts.
The diagnosis alone doesn’t determine the treatment.
A normal ultrasound doesn’t necessarily rule out PCOS.
A few pieces of information prepared ahead of time can help the professional understand your history and choose the most relevant tests.
How long have your cycles been irregular?
Have you noticed acne, unusual hair growth, or hair loss?
Is there a family history of PCOS or diabetes?
Do you wish to become pregnant in the short or medium term?
A small tip before the appointment
If possible, note the dates of your last period, the approximate length of your cycles, the symptoms you’re noticing, and any treatments or supplements you’re taking.
The essentials of the workup
The diagnosis relies on several factors, not a single test.
A blood test can look for certain hormonal imbalances and rule out other causes.
An ultrasound can complete the workup depending on the situation.
Results should always be interpreted by a healthcare professional.
Key takeaways
A PCOS workup isn’t a single test or a final verdict. It helps you understand your hormonal functioning, look for other possible causes, and build care that’s suited to your situation.
This article is for information only and doesn’t replace a medical consultation or the personalized interpretation of your test results.

PCOS • HORMONAL ACNE

Understanding
hormonal acne
7 min read
Guide
Beginner
Educational content
Why hormonal acne can appear with PCOS, how to recognize it, and what solutions may help manage it.
It affects many women and is neither a lack of hygiene nor an inevitability: understanding its origin helps manage it better.
In this article
What is hormonal acne?
Why can PCOS cause acne?
How to recognize hormonal acne
Hormonal acne and the menstrual cycle
What can help
When to see a doctor?
Key takeaways
What is hormonal acne?

Hormonal acne is a form of acne directly linked to hormonal fluctuations or an imbalance, particularly in androgens. Unlike the more typical acne of adolescence, it often affects adult women and can persist or appear after that period.
It is also distinguished by its location, its depth, and its tendency to reappear in the same spots despite a well-followed regular skincare routine.
Good to know
Hormonal acne is not linked to a lack of hygiene: washing your face more often does not make it go away, and may even irritate the skin.
Why can PCOS cause acne?

In PCOS, a relative excess of androgens stimulates the sebaceous glands, which then produce more sebum. Some skin is also more sensitive to these hormones, which explains why acne can be pronounced even without a major imbalance measured in a lab.
This is not a matter of willpower: this sensitivity varies from person to person and does not depend on your lifestyle habits.
How to recognize hormonal acne
Certain features often recur, though not systematically:
Lower face: jawline, chin
Deeper, sometimes painful breakouts
Often reappears in the same spots
Redness or marks that persist
Hormonal acne and the menstrual cycle

Hormonal acne can fluctuate throughout the cycle. Many women notice a flare-up in the days before their period, when progesterone rises and then drops sharply, temporarily stimulating sebum production.
Tracking your flare-ups
Noting when breakouts appear relative to your cycle can help you and your dermatologist better understand the hormonal link.
What can help
A few simple care habits can help limit flare-ups, without fully clearing them on their own:
Gently cleanse your skin morning and evening
Avoid harsh or stripping products
Protect your skin from the sun daily
Avoid squeezing or picking at breakouts
Depending on the situation, a dermatologist or gynecologist may suggest topical treatments (creams, gels) or, if needed, a suitable hormonal treatment.
No self-medicating
Treatments for hormonal acne (topical or hormonal) must be prescribed and monitored by a healthcare professional, particularly if you are hoping to conceive.
When to see a doctor?
Medical advice is especially helpful in certain situations:
Acne that persists despite suitable care
Painful or deep breakouts (nodules, cysts)
Severe acne or acne that worsens rapidly
Marks or scars that are settling in
Key takeaways
The essential points
Hormonal acne has an identifiable cause, linked to androgens.
It often affects the lower face and can worsen before your period.
It is neither a lack of hygiene nor an inevitability.
Gentle care and, if needed, a suitable treatment can improve it.
A dermatologist or gynecologist can support you if it persists.
A guide to better understanding
This article is for general information only and does not replace a medical consultation. If in doubt or if symptoms persist, seek advice from a healthcare professional.

PCOS • ESSENTIAL GUIDE

Understanding
PCOS
10 min read
Guide
Beginner
Educational content
Polycystic ovary syndrome, often called PCOS, is a common hormonal condition that can affect your cycles, ovulation, skin, hair, metabolism, and sometimes fertility.
How it shows up varies a lot from one woman to another. Understanding PCOS mainly helps you recognize its symptoms, know when to seek medical advice, and track how it evolves without self-blame.
In this article
What is PCOS?
Why does PCOS happen?
The main signs
How is it diagnosed?
PCOS and ovulation
PCOS and fertility
PCOS and weight / metabolism
Skin, hair, and body hair
How is PCOS managed?
Common misconceptions
When to see a doctor
Key takeaways
What is PCOS?
Polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) is a common hormonal condition that can change the ovaries’ usual functioning and the balance of certain hormones.
For some women, the main issue is irregular ovulation. For others, it’s acne, excess hair growth, hair loss, or metabolic signs that stand out first.
Good to know
Despite its name, PCOS doesn’t necessarily mean the ovaries contain “cysts.” The historical term can be misleading, and an ultrasound alone isn’t enough to make the diagnosis.
Why does PCOS happen?
There isn’t a single cause of PCOS. It appears to result from several factors that can combine: family predisposition, hormonal functioning, ovulation, metabolism, and individual factors.
Family predisposition and genetic factors
Disruptions in ovulation
Relative androgen excess
Insulin resistance in some women
Metabolic and environmental factors
PCOS is not a personal failing. It doesn’t simply result from a lack of willpower, poor diet, or insufficient physical activity.
The main signs
PCOS can show up very differently from one woman to another. Some have several symptoms, while others notice very few.
Irregular, widely spaced, or sometimes absent cycles
Irregular or hard-to-predict ovulation
Persistent acne, particularly on the lower face
Increased hair growth on the face, chest, or body
Hormonal-pattern hair loss
Weight gain or difficulty losing weight
Difficulty conceiving
Important
Having one of these symptoms doesn’t automatically mean you have PCOS. Several other conditions can cause similar symptoms.
How is it diagnosed?
Diagnosing PCOS is a medical process. A healthcare provider usually starts by discussing your cycles, symptoms, medical history, and any treatments you’re taking.
Depending on the situation, hormonal blood tests and an ultrasound may also be offered.
Irregular cycles or infrequent ovulation
Signs of androgen excess: acne, excess hair growth, hair loss, or blood test results
Ovarian appearance consistent with PCOS on ultrasound, when this exam is indicated
The doctor must also rule out other possible causes of irregular cycles or androgen excess before confirming a PCOS diagnosis.
PCOS and ovulation
Ovulation is the release of an egg (oocyte) from the ovary. In PCOS, ovulation can be less frequent or harder to predict.
This can explain why cycles are sometimes long, irregular, or hard to anticipate.
Tracking your cycle
Recording your period dates, symptoms, and any signs of ovulation can help you better understand your own patterns.
PCOS and fertility
Because ovulation can be irregular, some women with PCOS may have more difficulty conceiving.
This doesn’t mean, however, that PCOS automatically prevents pregnancy. Many women with PCOS conceive naturally or with appropriate medical support.
Keep in mind
Difficulty conceiving doesn’t mean it’s impossible. If you’re hoping to become pregnant, a doctor or midwife can suggest a strategy suited to your situation.
PCOS and weight / metabolism
PCOS can be associated with metabolic changes, including insulin resistance in some women.
However, weight alone cannot diagnose or rule out PCOS. A slim woman can have PCOS, just as a woman who is overweight may not have it.
Follow-up care should consider overall health, not just the number on the scale.
Skin, hair, and body hair
Relative androgen excess can affect the sebaceous glands and hair follicles.
Depending on the woman, this can show up as persistent acne, increased hair growth, or hair loss.
Hormonal acne
Increased facial or body hair
Thinning hair or hair loss
How is PCOS managed?
There is no single approach to managing PCOS that works for every woman. The choice depends on symptoms, goals, and medical circumstances.
The goal can differ depending on the stage of life: regulating cycles, improving certain symptoms, protecting metabolic health, or supporting a pregnancy plan.
Health-supporting habits
Eating a varied, regular diet suited to your needs
Engaging in regular physical activity that you can sustain over time
Maintaining sufficiently regular sleep
Tracking how your cycles and symptoms change over time
Not blaming yourself for changes in weight or symptoms
Depending on your needs, a healthcare provider may also offer treatments for certain symptoms or to support a pregnancy plan.
Don’t self-medicate
Hormonal treatments, metabolic medications, and dietary supplements should all be discussed with a healthcare provider.
Common misconceptions about PCOS
PCOS always means having “cysts”: the name can be misleading. The diagnosis doesn’t rely solely on the presence of cysts.
All women with PCOS are overweight: PCOS can affect women of all body types.
PCOS always prevents pregnancy: ovulation may be irregular, but pregnancy is still possible.
A single symptom is enough to diagnose PCOS: diagnosis requires a comprehensive evaluation.
PCOS simply goes away with age: how it presents can change over a lifetime, but ongoing follow-up remains important.
When to see a doctor
Medical advice is particularly worthwhile when cycles become very irregular, stop for several months, or when unusual symptoms appear.
Very irregular or absent cycles
Unusual acne or hair growth
Significant hair loss
Difficulty conceiving
Rapidly changing symptoms
Key takeaways
The essential points
PCOS is a common hormonal condition.
It can show up in many different ways.
Not all women with PCOS have the same symptoms.
Weight alone is not enough to diagnose or rule out PCOS.
Diagnosis requires a comprehensive medical evaluation.
PCOS can affect ovulation and sometimes fertility.
A personalized care approach helps meet each woman’s needs.
A guide to better understanding

This article is intended for general information and does not replace a medical consultation. Every situation is different: if in doubt or if symptoms persist, seek advice from a healthcare professional.

PCOS lifestyle and
management
7 min read
Guide
Beginner
Reviewed content
Management options for PCOS, and simple habits to support your everyday life.
In this article
Care built together with a professional
Balanced diet
Suitable physical activity
Sleep and stress management
Emotional well-being
Signs that call for prompt attention
Key takeaways
Favor fiber (vegetables, legumes, whole grains)
Spread meals out to avoid intense hunger
Limit fast sugars and highly processed foods
No food is off-limits: aim for overall balance rather than strict rules

There is no single treatment for PCOS: management is tailored to your symptoms, your priorities (cycle, fertility, skin, weight), and your personal situation. It can combine lifestyle measures, hormonal treatments, or other options depending on your needs.
Regular physical activity, even moderate (brisk walking, cycling, light strength training), helps support hormonal and metabolic balance. Consistency matters more than intensity.
Getting enough sleep and taking regular moments to relax help limit the impact of stress on hormonal balance, which can in turn influence PCOS symptoms.
Good to know
Small, lasting changes are often more effective in the long run than radical changes that are hard to maintain.

Living with PCOS can weigh on your mood, especially because of visible symptoms or worries about fertility. These feelings are valid: talking to someone close to you or to a professional is a full part of comprehensive care.
See a doctor if
Intense or unusual pelvic pain, very heavy or prolonged bleeding, extreme fatigue or unusual persistent thirst, or emotional distress that settles in over time.
Good to know
PCOS is managed day to day with simple habits and regular medical follow-up: every small adjustment counts, at your own pace.

Weight, metabolism, and
insulin resistance
6 min read
Guide
Intermediate
Reviewed content
The link between PCOS, weight, and insulin resistance — without judgment or shortcuts.
In this article
The link between PCOS and metabolism
Understanding insulin resistance
Weight: what’s true and what isn’t
Habits that support balance
When medical follow-up is helpful
Key takeaways
PCOS is often associated with metabolic changes, including insulin resistance. However, this association doesn’t concern only women who are overweight — metabolic profiles vary from person to person.
Insulin is a hormone that helps cells use the glucose in the blood. With insulin resistance, cells respond less well to this hormone, and the body may compensate by producing more insulin.
In PCOS, this can be associated with increased androgen production and may contribute to certain symptoms. But not all women with PCOS have the same metabolic profile.
Good to know
Insulin resistance can be checked through blood tests when the doctor considers it relevant. Whether tests are needed depends on your individual situation.
PCOS affects women of all body types, from slim to heavier builds.
Weight gain isn’t systematic.
Losing weight isn’t always necessary — or enough on its own — to improve symptoms.
A small weight loss can sometimes improve certain metabolic markers or cycle regularity when excess weight is present.
The goal isn’t to chase a “perfect” weight, but to build realistic, lasting habits. A balanced diet, movement, and regular sleep can all contribute to better metabolic health.
Regular, varied meals rich in fiber
Regular physical activity, even if moderate
Enough regular sleep
Enough daily hydration

Medical follow-up for PCOS isn’t limited to the cycle or hormonal symptoms. Depending on your profile, your healthcare provider may also monitor certain metabolic markers to help identify potential risk factors early.
Follow-up tailored to your profile
The workup isn’t the same for everyone.
Your doctor may decide to check certain markers based on your symptoms, your medical history, your family situation, and other risk factors.
What may be monitored
Blood glucose and/or HbA1c, depending on context
Lipid panel (cholesterol and triglycerides)
Blood pressure and cardiovascular risk assessment
Weight and waist circumference tracking, without judgment
Situations worth mentioning
Certain changes are worth mentioning during a consultation, especially when they’re new, persistent, or unusual for you.
Very irregular cycles
Mention periods that are very spaced out or unpredictable.
Thirst or frequent urination
Talk to your doctor if these signs appear in an unusual way.
Significant weight change
A rapid or unexplained change is worth getting evaluated.
Family history
Mention any family history of diabetes or metabolic conditions.
Please note

Unusual thirst, frequent urination, persistent fatigue, or a significant, unexplained change in weight should be reported to a healthcare professional. These signs can have several causes and don’t, on their own, confirm insulin resistance or diabetes.
Follow-up happens over time
Your doctor may suggest regular check-ups rather than a single workup. The goal is to adapt advice and tests to how you progress, without focusing solely on weight.
Good to know
Weight is only one part of the metabolic picture in PCOS. A comprehensive approach takes into account cycles, symptoms, lifestyle habits, medical history, and metabolic markers.
